newsitem.title: JAPAN: Some relief seen for Japan oil companies' profits.
newsitem.headline: Some relief seen for Japan oil companies' profits.

text.p: A marginal recovery in profits may be in store for Japan's beleaguered oil refining and marketing companies over the next fiscal year, analysts say.
The relief is likely to stem from a stronger yen, cost-cutting in crude procurement and distribution, lower plant maintenance costs and work force reductions, they said.

"The biggest plus for the oil firms' share prices in the immediate future is continued strength in the yen versus the dollar," said Craig Pennington, Asian oil and gas analyst for UBS Securities Ltd in Tokyo.

"But such a correlation is typically short-lived, and the relatively cheap product imports a strong yen brings is likely to foster competition which could in fact negatively impact company earnings," he added.

However, Japanese refiners will benefit from an April relaxation of refinery maintenance rules, which is expected to help plants cut costs through shorter closure times and a lighter workload for checkups, Pennington said.

The Ministry of International Trade and Industry's (MITI) new rules allow oil firms to run their plants for up to four years without major maintenance closures, compared with the previous upper limit of two years.
"Thanks to the new measures, we can probably keep our plants running 10 more days a year," a refinery official said.
The additional 20 working days in two years can be roughly translated into a three percent increase in operating rates, refiners said.
Refiners also point to recent signs of increased industry cooperation and consolidation as good news for their earnings.

In late April, Japan's Esso Sekiyu, General Sekiyu KK and Tonen announced they were discussing a cooperative arrangement involving their operations in the city of Kawasaki that would save the three Exxon Corp affiliates four billion yen.
The news followed a February announcement that Mitsubishi Oil Co Ltd and Showa Shell Sekiyu KK were planning to merge parts of their refinery and distribution systems.
Japan's oil product import market, previously dominated by refiners, was liberalised a year ago, allowing non-refiners to import petroleum products for the first time in ten years.
But a weak yen, high crude prices, and import tarrifs actually limited the influx of foreign products to little more than a trickle.
And expectations of high imports both before and during the deregulation led to a price war among gasoline retailers.

As a result, Japan's gross retail gasoline margin dropped 40 percent to 33 yen per litre in December 1996, from 55 yen per litre in April 1994, according to the Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics.
Japan's seven leading oil firms are Nippon Oil Co Ltd, Showa Shell Sekiyu KK, Mitsubishi Oil Co Ltd, Tonen Corp, Cosmo Oil Co Ltd, General Sekiyu KK and Japan Energy Corp.
Oil companies which follow the April to March business year, the common practice in Japan, are due to announce their earnings for the year ended March 31 later this week.

Analysts said lacklustre results for Tonen Corp and Showa Shell Sekiyu, which reported in February for the year ended December 31, may be early indications of the fiscal year result prospects of other oil firms.
Squeezed by margins, Showa Shell's parent current profits fell by 30 percent from a year earlier to 15.23 billion yen.

Tonen's parent current profits climbed to 17.02 billion yen, a 30 percent rise over an abysmal 1995 figure, but this was negated by a higher tax charge which reduced parent earnings per share by 24 percent, analysts said.
Current profit is pretax and includes gains or losses on non-operating activities such as investments in stocks.
-- Peter Lardner, Tokyo Energy Desk +813-5473-3708
